video.title: God Never Said RAINBOW. What "My Bow" Really Means in Genesis 9:13
video.description:
God never said "rainbow." In Genesis 9:13 He says, "I do set my bow in the cloud," and the Hebrew word, qeshet, is the word for a hunter's bow and a warrior's bow everywhere else in the Old Testament.

In this Bible study we read the sign of the covenant with Noah through the Hebrew text and the King James Version. We trace qeshet through Genesis, from Hagar's "bowshot" to Esau's hunting bow and Jacob's bow of war, and see how Israel described God in the storm as an archer whose arrows are lightning (Psalm 18, Habakkuk 3, Lamentations 2). We look at who the sign is really for, "I will look upon it, that I may remember" (Genesis 9:16), at why God made the promise while naming the evil of the human heart (Genesis 8:21), and at how Babylon's bow in the sky compares with Genesis. Then we follow the bow to Ezekiel's vision of the throne, to Isaiah 54, and to the rainbow around the throne in Revelation 4.

All Scripture quotations are from the King James Version.

Is there a dark cloud over your life right now? Share your thoughts in the comments, and subscribe for more studies beneath the verse.

transcript.text: Noah steps out onto ground that is still soft from the water.
Behind him stands the ark, empty now.
He builds an altar.
The smoke of the offering rises, and the text says the Lord smells it.
Then God speaks, and he points to the cloud.
Here's the question almost nobody asks: why a bow?
Of all the signs God could have chosen, why did he reach for a word that everywhere else in the Hebrew Bible means a weapon?
Because that is what the text says.
In Genesis chapter 9, verse 13, God does not say, rainbow.
There is no separate Hebrew word for rainbow in the whole Old Testament.
God says, I do set my bow in the cloud.
The Hebrew word is qeshet.
And qeshet is the word for the bow a hunter carries into the field and a soldier carries into battle.
So, here is the first layer of the answer: the sign of peace after the flood is a weapon, hung up in the sky.
God is not painting a decoration.
He is setting down his bow.
But there is a deeper layer under that.
Let us start where the text starts, Genesis chapter 9, verse 13.
I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth.
Read it slowly: my bow.
The Hebrew is qashti, which is simply qeshet with my attached to the end.
It is personal.
This is not a bow, it is his bow.
Now, if you read this in the King James Version, you are already ahead of most readers, because the King James keeps the word.
It says bow.
Many modern translations say rainbow, and that is not wrong as a description of what Noah saw.
But the moment a translation says rainbow, the weapon disappears.
The reader sees colors.
The original listener heard a bow.
So, let us see where else this word appears, and let us stay in Genesis first, so that we hear it the way the first readers of this book would have heard it.
Genesis chapter 21.
Hagar is in the wilderness with her son.
The water is gone.
She cannot bear to watch the boy die.
So she puts him under a bush and sits down.
And the text says, she sat a good way off, as it were, a bowshot.
That word bowshot is built on qeshet.
The distance is measured by how far an arrow flies.
A few verses later, in verse 20, the same boy grows up in the wilderness, and the text says he became an archer.
Again, the word is built on qeshet.
Genesis chapter 27, verse 3.

transcript.text: The one who looks at the bow is God.
The Hebrew word for remember there is zakar.
And it is the same word that turned the whole flood story around just one chapter earlier.
Genesis chapter 8 verse 1, and God remembered Noah.
In Hebrew, remembering is not simply recalling a fact.
It is turning your attention towards someone and acting on their behalf.
When God remembers Noah, the wind blows and the waters begin to go down.
So in chapter 9, God hangs his bow in the sky.
And he says, in effect, when the cloud comes back, I will look at my own bow and I will act on what I promised.
The sign is set where God will see it.
That does not mean God is forgetful.
The text is speaking in human language the way scripture often does.
But it tells you something about the kind of promise this is.
It does not rest on Noah's memory.
It does not rest on our memory.
It rests on God keeping his eyes on his own laid-down weapon.
Now notice how wide this promise is.
In verses 8 through 17, the phrase every living creature appears four times.
And the word covenant appears seven times in those same 10 verses.
The covenant is not with one family only.
It is with Noah, his sons, the birds, the cattle, every beast of the earth.
Verse 10.
List them out.
In its reach, it may be the widest covenant in the whole Bible.
It covers everything that breathes.
The word for the token in verse 13 is also worth stopping on.
The Hebrew is oht.
It means a sign, a mark, a visible pledge.
And it appears again at two other great moments in the law.
In Genesis chapter 17 verse 11, God says of circumcision,
It shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you.
Same word.
And in Exodus chapter 31 verse 13, God says of the Sabbath,
It is a sign between me and you throughout your generations.
Same word again.
But look at the difference.
Circumcision is something Abraham's family does.
The Sabbath is something Israel keeps.
The bow is the only one of these great signs that no human being does anything to make.
No one hangs it.
No one keeps it.
God puts it there, and God looks at it.
Now we come to the question underneath all of this.
Why would God promise this at all?
You would expect the promise to come because people had changed.
The flood washed the earth.
Surely humanity is better now.
But the text says the opposite, and it says it on purpose.
Go back to Genesis chapter 6 verse 5, the reason for the flood.
And God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.
Now read Genesis chapter 8 verse 21, the moment just before the bow.
And the Lord smelled a sweet savor.
And the Lord said in his heart, I will not again curse the ground anymore for man's sake;
for the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth; neither will I again smite any more everything living, as I have done.
Read those two verses side by side.
The diagnosis is the same.
The imagination of the human heart is evil.

transcript.text: And there was a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald.
REVELATION 4:3
Here the King James finally uses the word rainbow, and there is a reason.
The Greek word John uses is i-e-r-i-s. It means a rainbow, the arc of colors itself.
That is interesting because the Greek translation of the Old Testament, the Septuagint, used a different word back in Genesis chapter 9.
It translated keshet with the Greek word toxon, which means an archer's bow.
If that word sounds familiar, it should.
Our English word toxic comes from the same Greek family, from the poison that was put on the tips of arrows.
So the Greek reader of Genesis read about God's warbow, and John, describing heaven, uses the word for a rainbow in colors of emerald green.
Many readers have taken that as the same sign, now seen in its full glory, with the language of the weapon softened into the language of light.
We should not press the change of word too far.
John may simply be describing what he saw, but the picture he gives is unmistakable.
Around the throne of the God who will judge the world is the bow of the covenant.
And look at what John sees next in chapter 5.
In the midst of that same throne, he sees a lamb as it had been slain.
The throne that is surrounded by the bow has a slain lamb at its center.
The text does not explain the connection for us in so many words, and we should not force it.
But place the two images side by side.
The bow that was hung up after judgement surrounds the throne, and at the centre of the throne is the one who bore judgment.
The word rainbow appears one more time in Revelation, in chapter 10, verse 1.
"And I saw another mighty angel come down from heaven, clothed with a cloud, and a rainbow was upon his head."
Even in the middle of a book full of judgements, the cloud comes down, and the bow is still there.
Now there is one more voice we need to hear before we pull this together, and it may be the most tender of them all.
Isaiah chapter 54.
God is speaking to his people, after exile, after loss, after a long season when it felt as though he had turned away.
And he reaches back to Noah, verse 9.
"For this is as the waters of Noah unto me; for as I have sworn that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth, so have I sworn that I would not be wroth with thee, nor rebuke thee."
Verse 10.
"For the mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed, but my kindness shall not depart from thee, neither shall the covenant of my peace be removed, saith the Lord that hath mercy on thee."
Do you see what Isaiah does?
He takes the promise made to Noah and uses it as the measure of God's faithfulness.

transcript.text: The rest of scripture still speaks of God as judge and the New Testament says so plainly.
What the bow tells us is not that judgment is gone, but that God has bound himself by his own word and that he holds his power under his promise.
That is exactly what a laid-down weapon means.
A weapon that has been destroyed tells you nothing about the one who owned it.
A weapon that has been hung up, still strong, still within reach, tells you everything.
It tells you the owner is able and has chosen not to.
Let us pull this together.
The Hebrew text never uses a word for rainbow, it says key shet, my bow.
And every other time that word appears in Genesis, it is a weapon for hunting or for war.
Across the Old Testament, God in the storm is described as an archer whose arrows are lightning.
The flood was his judgment from the sky, and when the sky clouds over again, God hangs his bow in the very place the storm comes from.
The sign is for God to look upon. It is his remembering, not ours, that holds the world.
He makes the promise knowing that the human heart has not changed, which means the promise rests on him alone.
Jewish tradition blessed God when the bow appeared, as the one who remembers.
Ezekiel saw that bow surrounding the glory of the Lord, Isaiah used it as the measure of God's unshakable kindness, and John saw it around the throne in heaven with a slain lamb at the centre.
So what does this mean for you right now?
First, notice that the sign is not asking you to hold the promise up.
Many of us live as though God's faithfulness depends on how well we remember it, how strongly we believe it, how steady we feel.
Verse 16 says God looks at the bow so that he may remember.
On your weakest day, the promise is still being kept from his side.
Second, notice that God made this promise while looking clearly at the human heart.
He did not wait for Noah's family to prove they were better.
He named the evil of the heart in the same sentence where he promised mercy.
If you have ever wondered whether God's kindness toward you is only good until he sees you clearly, Genesis 8:21 answers that. He saw clearly, and he hung up his bow.
Third, notice where the bow appears, not in a clear sky, in the cloud.
The sign shows up inside the very thing that frightens you.
The storm is not proof that the promise has failed. It is the place where the promise was always meant to be seen.
And maybe the part that stays with me most is this.
